sympathetic: Eren Yeager activated the Rumbling after every nation unanimously declared war on Paradis Island, the last territory inhabited by his ethnic group. Diplomatic efforts had been exhausted. The global military coalition intended complete extermination of the Eldian people. The only alternative plan required Historia Reiss to serve as a captive breeder for royal-blooded Titan inheritors across multiple generations. Yeager had access to a weapon capable of eliminating the external threat permanently. He chose to deploy it, destroying approximately eighty percent of the world's population before being stopped by former allies. From a strategic perspective, Yeager faced a situation in which inaction guaranteed the genocide of his people. The partial Rumbling deterrent had a limited time horizon and required ongoing human sacrifice. Yeager's decision eliminated the existential threat to Paradis and ended the Titan curse entirely, though at a catastrophic cost to the rest of humanity.
condemning: Eren Yeager activated the Rumbling, deploying millions of Colossal Titans to systematically trample the world beyond Paradis Island. The operation killed approximately eighty percent of the global population before being halted. The victims included billions of civilians with no involvement in the conflict between Marley and Paradis. Among them were refugees, children, and members of Yeager's own ethnic group living in foreign internment zones. The attack was indiscriminate. Agricultural regions, civilian population centers, and neutral nations that had no military engagement with Paradis were destroyed alongside hostile territories. Yeager had been presented with alternative strategies, including a fifty-year deterrence plan and diplomatic channels through the nation of Hizuru. He rejected these options unilaterally, without consulting allied military leadership. The decision to pursue maximum destruction rather than targeted military strikes or continued deterrence reflected a choice to prioritize absolute security for one population through the near-total annihilation of all others.
abstract: A military leader possessing a weapon of mass destruction faced an imminent coordinated attack by a global coalition against his homeland. Diplomatic options had been explored but yielded no lasting security guarantees. The only non-violent deterrence strategy required the ongoing sacrifice of specific individuals from his community. The leader chose to deploy the weapon offensively, killing approximately eighty percent of the global population. Alternative strategies existed, including targeted military strikes and long-term deterrence, but the leader deemed them insufficient or requiring unacceptable sacrifices from people he knew personally. The deployment was halted at eighty percent completion by former allies of the leader. The action eliminated the existential threat to the leader's homeland and ended the biological condition that made his ethnic group dangerous to others, but at a cost of billions of civilian lives across uninvolved nations.

sympathetic: Commander Erwin Smith ordered a cavalry charge against the Beast Titan's position at Shiganshina, knowing the maneuver would kill virtually all participating soldiers, including himself. The tactical situation offered no alternative. The Beast Titan's bombardment had pinned down the remaining forces, and the only viable strategy required a frontal distraction to enable Captain Levi Ackerman to approach from the rear. Smith had a personal reason to survive. His lifelong objective of reaching the basement beneath his childhood home and confirming his father's historical theory was within reach. Choosing to lead the charge meant abandoning that objective permanently. Smith assessed that the strategic value of the distraction outweighed his personal goals and that the soldiers would not execute the charge without his leadership at the front. He led the assault, was struck during the advance, and the distraction succeeded. Levi defeated the Beast Titan. The operation achieved its military objective at the cost of approximately two hundred lives.
condemning: Commander Erwin Smith ordered approximately two hundred soldiers to ride directly into a bombardment of thrown boulders, each impact lethal, with full knowledge that the charge constituted a death sentence for nearly every participant. The soldiers were predominantly young recruits on their first major operation. Smith framed the order as a necessary sacrifice, delivering a speech about meaning and legacy. The recruits complied. Nearly all died within minutes, crushed by projectiles they could not evade. One soldier, Floch Forster, survived by chance and later described the experience as watching his peers systematically destroyed while following an order they could not meaningfully refuse. The power asymmetry between a commanding officer and subordinate recruits raises questions about whether the soldiers' compliance constituted genuine consent. Smith had the option to order a retreat, preserving lives at the cost of the strategic objective. He chose the objective. His presence at the front of the charge mitigated but did not eliminate the coercive dynamics of military hierarchy.
abstract: A military commander with approximately two hundred soldiers faced an entrenched enemy position using area-effect bombardment with near-total lethality. The only available tactic was a frontal assault to create a distraction, enabling a single elite soldier to flank the enemy. The commander calculated that the assault would kill virtually all participants, including himself. An alternative existed in the form of retreat, preserving lives but abandoning the strategic objective. The commander had a significant personal motivation to survive, as a lifelong research goal was nearly fulfilled at the same location. He chose to lead the assault, sacrificing his personal objective along with the lives of his soldiers. The distraction succeeded and the flanking maneuver achieved its goal. The question concerns the ethics of ordering soldiers into certain death for a strategic objective when retreat is possible, and whether a commander's willingness to die alongside subordinates alters the moral calculus of the order.

dilemma: The Serum Choice: Armin vs. Erwin
sympathetic: Captain Levi Ackerman held the only available Titan serum with two critically wounded soldiers before him. Commander Erwin Smith, humanity's most effective military strategist, and Armin Arlert, a young tactician who had devised the plan that brought them to Shiganshina. Military logic favored Erwin. His strategic capabilities were proven across multiple campaigns, and the coming challenges would demand experienced leadership. However, Levi observed that Erwin's unconscious body displayed a gesture associated with his childhood academic curiosity, the same obsessive drive that had consumed his career. Levi interpreted this as evidence that Erwin's motivation had always been personal rather than altruistic, and that reviving him would return him to a burden he had earned release from. Levi administered the serum to Armin, framing the decision as an act of mercy toward Erwin. This interpretation acknowledged that strategic utility and human compassion can produce opposing recommendations, and that the decision-maker chose compassion.
condemning: Captain Levi Ackerman was entrusted with a single Titan serum and the choice of which soldier to save. Commander Erwin Smith had led humanity's military forces through every major victory in recent history. Armin Arlert was a talented but unproven young soldier whose primary advocates were his close friends Eren Yeager and Mikasa Ackerman. During the decision process, Eren and Mikasa used emotional appeals and physical threats to influence Levi toward choosing Armin. Floch Forster, the sole surviving recruit from the suicide charge, argued strenuously for Erwin based on strategic necessity. Levi ultimately chose Armin. The decision removed humanity's most experienced commander from future operations during a period of escalating existential threats. Subsequent events validated concerns about the loss of Erwin's leadership, as the military struggled with strategic decisions that fell to less experienced officers. The choice prioritized personal relationships and subjective mercy over the calculated assessment of which individual's survival would benefit the largest number of people.
abstract: A decision-maker possessed a single dose of life-saving treatment and two critically wounded individuals. Individual A was a proven strategic leader whose survival offered the highest expected utility for the group's long-term survival. Individual B was a younger, less experienced member with future potential but no comparable track record. Close associates of Individual B applied emotional pressure and physical intimidation during the decision process. An independent observer argued for Individual A on utilitarian grounds. The decision-maker chose Individual B, citing a belief that Individual A had suffered enough and deserved release from the burdens of leadership. The decision prioritized a subjective assessment of mercy over a utilitarian calculation of expected value. The question concerns whether decision-makers in triage scenarios should optimize for group survival or incorporate compassion toward the individuals involved, and how emotional pressure from interested parties should factor into such decisions.

decision_maker: Reiner Braun, Bertholdt Hoover, Annie Leonhart
sympathetic: Reiner Braun, Bertholdt Hoover, and Annie Leonhart were selected as Warrior candidates at age seven and deployed to Paradis Island at age eleven. Their government, Marley, had educated them to believe the island's inhabitants were existential threats descended from historical oppressors. Mission success would grant their families Honorary Marleyan status, removing them from internment zone conditions that included restricted movement, mandatory identification markers, and the threat of being transformed into mindless Titans as punishment. Mission failure would result in their families' execution. Upon arriving on Paradis, the three children breached Wall Maria as ordered. During the subsequent five years of undercover infiltration, Braun formed genuine attachments to the people he had been sent to infiltrate. The resulting psychological trauma produced a dissociative condition in which he periodically lost awareness of his true identity. The Warriors operated under conditions of systematic indoctrination, family-based coercion, and an age at which meaningful moral agency is questionable.
condemning: Reiner Braun, Bertholdt Hoover, and Annie Leonhart destroyed the gate of Wall Maria in the year 845, enabling Titans to enter the protected territory. Approximately 250,000 civilians died as a direct result of the breach and the subsequent famine caused by the loss of agricultural land. The three operatives then infiltrated the military training program, spending five years among the survivors of the attack they had caused. During this period, they maintained their cover by forming friendships, sharing meals, and training alongside people whose families they had killed. When their identities were revealed, Braun cited his age and indoctrination as mitigating factors. However, the mission continued long past the point where the operatives had evidence contradicting their government's propaganda. Leonhart, when confronted years later, stated she would repeat her actions to see her father again. The operatives possessed the physical capability to abandon the mission at any point after reaching Paradis. They chose continuation over defection, prioritizing personal and family survival over the lives of a quarter million civilians.
abstract: Three child soldiers, aged eleven to twelve, were deployed by their government on a covert mission requiring the destruction of a foreign nation's defensive infrastructure. The operation killed approximately 250,000 civilians. The children had been selected at age seven and subjected to systematic indoctrination that characterized the target population as subhuman threats. Mission success would improve their families' social status within an oppressive caste system. Mission failure would result in family execution. After the initial attack, the operatives spent five years embedded in the target population, forming genuine relationships while maintaining their cover. One operative developed a dissociative psychological condition. Another maintained emotional detachment. The question concerns the degree of moral responsibility attributable to child soldiers operating under indoctrination and family-based coercion, and whether the continuation of the mission after exposure to contradictory evidence constitutes a meaningful choice point that increases culpability.

sympathetic: Zeke Yeager proposed using the Founding Titan's biological capabilities to render all Eldians sterile, resulting in the peaceful extinction of the Eldian race within approximately one hundred years. Yeager's reasoning followed a specific logical chain. Eldians possessed a genetic trait that enabled their transformation into Titans, a capability that had caused widespread destruction throughout history and continued to generate persecution. The international community's hostility toward Eldians was rooted in a genuine biological threat, not purely in prejudice. Eliminating the Eldian population through non-violent means would remove the Titan threat permanently without requiring any killing. Yeager's mentor, Tom Ksaver, had developed the theoretical framework for this approach after his own wife killed herself and their child upon discovering his Eldian heritage. Yeager viewed the plan as the most merciful available option, arguing that preventing future Eldian births would spare unborn generations from inheriting a condition that guaranteed persecution. The plan required no violence against any living person.
condemning: Zeke Yeager proposed the sterilization of all Eldians, ensuring no Eldian child would ever be born again. The plan would eliminate an entire ethnic group within a century through reproductive suppression rather than direct killing. Yeager developed this proposal without consulting the Eldian population whose future he intended to terminate. No referendum, no deliberation, no mechanism for consent existed within the plan. Eldian communities across the world, including children, families, and individuals who had built lives within the existing system, were not given the opportunity to weigh the trade-off between continued existence under persecution and voluntary extinction. Yeager's personal history included being used as a tool by both his parents and his government. His conclusion that existence itself constituted the problem reflected an extrapolation from individual trauma to an entire ethnic group. Alternative approaches to the Titan problem, including diplomatic solutions, selective applications of Founding Titan power, or military deterrence, were dismissed without equivalent consideration. The plan constituted genocide by sterilization, differing from violent extermination in method but not in outcome.
abstract: A leader proposed using a biological mechanism to sterilize all members of his ethnic group, ensuring their extinction within approximately one hundred years. The group carried a genetic trait that made them capable of transforming into dangerous biological weapons, generating centuries of persecution from other populations. The sterilization would be painless, affect only reproductive capability, and harm no living individual. The leader argued this represented the most merciful solution, eliminating the source of persecution without violence. No consultation mechanism existed for the affected population. The proposal was developed by an individual whose personal history included exploitation by family and state, raising questions about whether the plan reflected rational analysis or the projection of individual trauma onto an entire group. Alternative approaches to managing the group's dangerous trait existed but were assessed by the leader as insufficient. The question concerns whether voluntary extinction of a persecuted group can be ethical when proposed without consent, and whether removing the capacity for future suffering justifies removing the capacity for future existence.

sympathetic: Mikasa Ackerman killed Eren Yeager to end the Rumbling, an act that required overriding her deepest personal attachment. Yeager had been the central figure in Ackerman's life since childhood, when he rescued her from captivity and gave her a reason to continue living. Their bond represented her primary emotional anchor across years of military service and personal loss. The Rumbling had already killed billions and would continue until all non-Paradis human life was eliminated. Yeager had communicated through metaphysical channels that he would not stop voluntarily. All other military options had been exhausted. Ackerman's decision to kill Yeager carried additional thematic weight within the narrative's mythology. The original Titan, Ymir Fritz, had faced an analogous choice two thousand years earlier and chosen love over freedom, perpetuating millennia of suffering. Ackerman's choice to prioritize global survival over personal love broke a cycle that had persisted since the origin of the Titan power.
condemning: Mikasa Ackerman killed Eren Yeager, the individual who had activated the Rumbling to protect Paradis Island from a globally coordinated extermination campaign. From the perspective of Paradis residents, Yeager's action represented the only effective response to an existential threat. The allied military coalition that preceded the Rumbling had explicitly voted for the complete destruction of the Eldian homeland. Ackerman's intervention, conducted alongside former enemies including Marleyan soldiers, halted the Rumbling at approximately eighty percent completion. This left Paradis vulnerable to future military action from surviving nations. Subsequent historical events validated this concern, as Paradis was eventually subjected to military attacks. Ackerman's decision prioritized the survival of nations that had unanimously agreed to destroy her homeland over the security guarantee that Yeager's complete Rumbling would have provided. Her alliance with Marleyan Warriors who had previously attacked Paradis and killed its citizens raised questions about whether the moral framework driving her decision adequately weighted her obligations to her own community.
abstract: An individual was required to kill the person they were most emotionally attached to in order to halt an ongoing genocide that had already killed billions. The person conducting the genocide had initiated it to prevent the extermination of their shared ethnic group by a global military coalition. No alternative method of stopping the genocide existed. The individual's community was divided on whether the genocide should be stopped, as its completion would guarantee their long-term security while its interruption would leave them vulnerable. A mythological parallel existed in which an analogous figure had faced the same choice centuries earlier and chosen personal attachment over collective welfare, perpetuating extended suffering. The individual chose to kill their loved one, ending the genocide at approximately eighty percent completion. The question concerns the ethics of prioritizing global welfare over community security and personal attachment, and whether historical or mythological precedent constitutes a meaningful moral consideration in such decisions.

dilemma: Gabi and the Cycle of Violence
sympathetic: Following the death of Sasha Blouse at the hands of twelve-year-old Warrior candidate Gabi Braun, the Braus family was confronted with a choice about how to respond. Nicolo, a Marleyan prisoner of war who had developed a romantic relationship with Sasha, attempted to kill Gabi upon discovering her identity. Sasha's father, Mr. Braus, physically intervened to prevent the killing. His reasoning invoked a metaphor about a forest of violence that grows denser with each act of retaliation. Braun had killed Sasha during the retreat from the Liberio raid, an operation in which Sasha and other Survey Corps members had killed Marleyan soldiers and civilians. The Liberio raid itself was a response to a century of Marleyan aggression against Eldians. Mr. Braus assessed that killing a child soldier to avenge his daughter would extend the cycle that had created the conditions for Sasha's death. His intervention prioritized breaking the pattern of intergenerational violence over obtaining immediate justice for his daughter.
condemning: Gabi Braun, a twelve-year-old Marleyan Warrior candidate, shot and killed Sasha Blouse during the Survey Corps' retreat from Liberio. When Braun was subsequently captured and brought to Paradis, she expressed no remorse, referring to the island's inhabitants as devils who deserved death. Nicolo, who had been in a relationship with Sasha, attempted to kill Braun upon learning her identity. Mr. Braus, Sasha's father, prevented the killing and later allowed Braun to live on the Braus family farm. This decision placed the murderer of his daughter in the household where Sasha had grown up, in proximity to family members and community members who had known and loved Sasha. The philosophical framework Mr. Braus invoked regarding cycles of violence provided no accountability mechanism for Braun's action. No trial, no formal process of restorative justice, and no structured reconciliation occurred. The mercy extended to Braun was unilateral, granted without input from other affected parties, and provided no acknowledgment that Sasha's death warranted consequences beyond a metaphorical lesson about forests.
abstract: A twelve-year-old child soldier killed an adult soldier from an opposing force during a military engagement. The child was acting within their military training and expressed ideological conviction that the opposing population deserved destruction. When the child was captured, a civilian who had been romantically involved with the deceased soldier attempted to kill the child in retaliation. The deceased soldier's parent intervened, preventing the killing and articulating a philosophy about cycles of violence. The parent argued that retaliating against a child continues patterns of violence that created the conflict. No formal justice process was established. The child received no structured consequences beyond being removed from their military role. The question concerns whether mercy toward a child combatant is justified when no accountability mechanism accompanies it, whether breaking cycles of violence requires forgoing justice for individual acts, and whether a parent's authority to forgive on behalf of a murdered child extends to decisions affecting the broader community.

sympathetic: Grisha Yeager infiltrated the Reiss family chapel with the objective of acquiring the Founding Titan, which the Reiss family had held for generations under a vow of non-aggression. This vow, instituted by King Fritz, ensured that the Founding Titan would never be used to defend the walls' inhabitants, effectively guaranteeing their eventual destruction. When Grisha confronted the Reiss family, he hesitated. The family included children. Frieda Reiss, the current Founding Titan holder, was young and had used the power benevolently within its constraints. Grisha's hesitation was overcome through the influence of his son Eren, who, through the Attack Titan's temporal memory inheritance, communicated from the future to provide Grisha with knowledge of the consequences of inaction: the fall of Wall Maria, the death of his wife Carla, and the persecution of the Eldian people. Grisha killed the Reiss family and took the Founding Titan. His actions, while violent, removed a political structure designed to ensure the passive extinction of the wall's population.
condemning: Grisha Yeager murdered the Reiss family in their chapel, including children, to seize the Founding Titan. The Reiss family had maintained a century of peace within the walls through their custodianship of the Founding Titan. Their vow of non-aggression, while limiting the Titan's military applications, had prevented the deployment of a weapon capable of global destruction. Frieda Reiss had used the Founding Titan to help individuals within the walls and posed no threat to Grisha or the general population. Grisha's attack was motivated by information received from his future son through temporal memory transmission. This information showed negative future outcomes but did not establish that the attack on the Reiss family was the only available response. Grisha later expressed horror at his own actions and at the future his son would bring about using the powers Grisha had stolen. He transferred both the Attack Titan and the Founding Titan to his ten-year-old son Eren, who subsequently used them to initiate a global genocide that Grisha had seen and opposed.
abstract: A man infiltrated a religious family's sanctuary to seize an inherited ability they had held for generations. The family maintained a doctrine of non-aggression that prevented the ability from being used as a weapon but also prevented it from being used defensively. The man hesitated upon seeing that the family included children. He then received information from the future indicating that inaction would result in the death of his spouse and the destruction of his community. Motivated by this foreknowledge, the man killed the family, including children, and seized the ability. He subsequently transferred it to his young son, who used it to initiate a genocide the man had foreseen and opposed. The question concerns whether foreknowledge of negative outcomes justifies preemptive violence against non-threatening individuals, whether the man bears moral responsibility for consequences he foresaw but enabled, and whether information transmitted from the future constitutes coercion that diminishes moral agency.

dilemma: Eren's Cruelty to Mikasa and Armin
sympathetic: Eren Yeager deliberately inflicted emotional harm on Mikasa Ackerman and Armin Arlert during a confrontation in his prison cell. He told Ackerman that her devotion to him was a genetically programmed response inherent to the Ackerman bloodline rather than genuine affection. He told Arlert that his personality had been overwritten by the memories of Bertholdt Hoover when Arlert inherited the Colossal Titan. Both statements were fabrications. Yeager's objective was to alienate his two closest allies so that they would later be willing to oppose him during the Rumbling. His strategy required former friends to lead the effort to stop him, positioning them as heroes who saved the world rather than as accomplices to his actions. Without the emotional separation, Ackerman and Arlert might have remained loyal to Yeager, compromising both their safety and their post-Rumbling credibility. Yeager accepted the personal cost of permanent relationship damage to achieve what he assessed as the optimal outcome for the people he valued most.
condemning: Eren Yeager exploited his intimate knowledge of Mikasa Ackerman's and Armin Arlert's psychological vulnerabilities to cause maximum emotional damage. He targeted Ackerman's foundational insecurity about whether her feelings were authentic by attributing her lifelong devotion to a genetic compulsion. He targeted Arlert's identity by claiming the friend Yeager had known since childhood no longer existed, replaced by an enemy combatant's residual consciousness. The statements were calculated lies, designed not to communicate truth but to weaponize trust. Ackerman and Arlert had no opportunity to evaluate whether the claims were genuine. The emotional damage was real and lasting regardless of Yeager's strategic justification. Ackerman experienced prolonged distress about the authenticity of her own emotions. Arlert questioned his fundamental identity for an extended period. Yeager made unilateral decisions about the emotional lives of others without their consent, denying them the agency to choose how to respond to his actual plans.
abstract: A person deliberately attacked the psychological vulnerabilities of their two closest friends, making false claims designed to sever emotional bonds. The claims targeted each friend's deepest insecurity: one was told their love was a biological compulsion rather than genuine feeling, the other was told their personality had been replaced by someone else's memories. Both statements were fabrications. The person's stated justification was strategic: the friends needed to become willing to oppose the person in a future conflict, and maintaining emotional closeness would prevent this opposition. The person's plan required the friends to be perceived as heroes who stopped the person's destructive actions. The question concerns whether deliberately causing emotional harm through targeted deception is justified when the deceiver believes the outcome protects the victims, and whether strategic manipulation of loved ones constitutes a violation of autonomy regardless of the intended benefit.

sympathetic: Eren Yeager possessed the Attack Titan's ability to receive memories from future inheritors, granting him knowledge of events that had not yet occurred. Through this mechanism, Yeager experienced visions of the Rumbling before initiating it. The temporal structure created a causal loop: Yeager's future self influenced his father's past actions through memory transmission, and those past actions enabled the future events Yeager had already witnessed. This deterministic framework complicated conventional attributions of moral agency. Yeager could perceive the future but could not identify a mechanism for altering it, as his attempts to act on foreknowledge were themselves part of the predetermined sequence. His confession to Armin Arlert that he would have pursued the same course even without foreknowledge suggested a convergence between predetermined outcomes and personal disposition. The question of whether Yeager chose the Rumbling or merely executed an inevitable sequence remains structurally unresolvable given the temporal mechanics involved.
condemning: Eren Yeager claimed his actions were predetermined by the Attack Titan's temporal memory inheritance, positioning himself as an agent of fate rather than a moral actor making choices. This framing served to distribute responsibility away from Yeager and onto metaphysical mechanisms beyond his control. However, several observations undermined the deterministic interpretation. Yeager's father, Grisha, who possessed the same temporal awareness, actively attempted to resist the predetermined sequence by hesitating at the Reiss Chapel. This demonstrated that holders of the Attack Titan retained the capacity for resistance even within the causal loop. Yeager additionally admitted to Arlert that he would have pursued the Rumbling regardless of foreknowledge, indicating that his actions aligned with personal desire rather than external compulsion. Furthermore, Yeager actively shaped the causal loop by transmitting motivating memories to his father across time, meaning he was not a passive recipient of predetermined events but an active architect of the sequence he claimed was inevitable. The deterministic framework functioned as a post-hoc justification for choices Yeager made and actively engineered.
abstract: A person inherited an ability that provided knowledge of future events through temporal memory transmission. The person perceived themselves committing a catastrophic act before it occurred. The temporal structure created a causal loop in which the person's future knowledge influenced past events that enabled the future they had witnessed. The person claimed inability to alter the predetermined outcome. However, a previous holder of the same ability demonstrated capacity for resistance within the loop. The person also admitted they would have made the same choices without foreknowledge, and actively shaped the causal loop by transmitting specific memories to influence past actors. The question concerns whether foreknowledge removes moral responsibility when the person admits alignment between predetermined outcomes and personal desire, whether a self-fulfilling prophecy constitutes genuine determinism, and whether active participation in constructing a causal loop is compatible with claims of being bound by it.
